items.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection - Information security management systems - Requirements
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC)
items.applicability: Any organisation of any size that wants a systematic, demonstrable way of managing information security risk, whether for certification, customer assurance or internal discipline. It sets out the ISMS requirements - context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation and improvement - plus a 93-control reference set in Annex A. It is a management system standard: conformity is demonstrated by audit against clauses 4 to 10 and the statement of applicability, not by implementing every Annex A control.
items.notes: Supersedes ISO/IEC 27001:2013. The 2022 revision replaced the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle with a Plan-Deliver-Maintain structure, added clause 4.4 (applicable requirements) and clause 4.5 (risk assessment), and reorganised Annex A from 114 to 93 controls with cloud, telework and data-quality themes added. Transition from 2013 ran to 31 October 2025, so most accredited certificates are now 2022-based; confirm the transition status of any specific certificate with the certification body.

items.title: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 - Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection - Information security controls
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC)
items.applicability: Guidance for the 93 Annex A controls of ISO/IEC 27001:2022, including a five-level implementation model and a control-attribute scheme covering purpose, applicability, implementation, information security properties and the risks addressed. It is the working reference for designing, documenting and testing controls. It is guidance rather than requirements: ISO/IEC 27002 cannot be certified, and Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001 remains a curated subset of the full catalogue.
items.notes: Supersedes ISO/IEC 27002:2013. New topics include data masking, data disclosure, web content filtering, data leakage prevention and security in the use of cloud services; several 2013 controls were removed or merged. Mapping a 2013-era control set to 2022 requires the removed-controls crosswalk in the standard's annexes rather than a straight renumbering.

items.title: ISO/IEC 27005:2018 - Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection - Information security risk management
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC)
items.applicability: Guidance on how to run information security risk assessment and risk treatment inside an information security management system, with a risk identification, analysis, evaluation and treatment process and an example of risk criteria. It is aimed at practitioners building the risk inputs to clause 4.5 of ISO/IEC 27001:2022. It is not a requirements standard and confers no certification.
items.notes: Supersedes ISO/IEC 27005:2009. The 2018 edition was aligned to the structure of ISO/IEC 27001:2013 (Annex A.3 risk management); a revision aligned with ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4.5 has been discussed for some years and ISO has signalled work on it, so confirm the edition on the ISO catalogue before citing clause-level text in a statement of applicability.

items.title: ISO/IEC 27003:2018 and ISO/IEC 27004:2022 - ISMS implementation, monitoring and measurement guidance
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC)
items.applicability: Two companion standards to ISO/IEC 27001. ISO/IEC 27003:2018 explains how to plan, implement, maintain and improve an ISMS, including the risk assessment and statement of applicability that practitioners most often struggle with. ISO/IEC 27004:2022 explains how to monitor, measure, analyse and evaluate the ISMS to satisfy clause 9 of ISO/IEC 27001. Both are guidance, not certifiable requirements, and both are written for organisations that already hold or are preparing for ISO/IEC 27001 certification.
items.notes: ISO/IEC 27003:2018 superseded ISO/IEC 27003:2009; ISO/IEC 27004:2022 superseded ISO/IEC 27004:2016 and the withdrawn ISO/IEC 27004:2009 (which was a measurement guide) and aligns to the 2022 revision of ISO/IEC 27001. Companion page for ISO/IEC 27004:2022 is https://www.iso.org/standard/79453.html.

items.title: ISO 19011:2018 and ISO/IEC 27006-1:2021 - Auditing of management systems and requirements for ISMS certification bodies
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC)
items.applicability: ISO 19011:2018 is the general standard for auditing any management system, covering audit principles, programme management and audit process; it is the reference internal auditors and ISMS certification bodies apply to plan, run and report an audit. ISO/IEC 27006-1:2021 sets the specific requirements an accredited certification body must meet to audit and certify an ISMS. Together they define the evidence rules that an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate ultimately rests on.
items.notes: ISO 19011:2018 superseded ISO 19011:2002 and the ISO 19011-1, -2 and -3 series, and deliberately dropped the audit programme guidance that ISO 19011-2 used to contain. ISO/IEC 27006-1:2021 superseded ISO/IEC 27006-1:2013 and is read together with IAF MD 26 for accredited certification. Companion page for ISO/IEC 27006-1:2021 is https://www.iso.org/standard/72023.html.

items.title: ISO/IEC 27701:2019 - Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection - Privacy information management system - Requirements
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC)
items.applicability: A privacy information management system (PIMS) for organisations that process personal data and need to demonstrate accountability for it, typically controllers and processors subject to data protection law. It reuses the ISO/IEC 27001 structure and adds a privacy-specific Annex A (P-1.1 to P-8.4) covering roles, lawful processing, privacy notices, data subject rights, records of processing, processor contracts and privacy impact assessment. It can be certified jointly with ISO/IEC 27001.
items.notes: Published shortly after the GDPR became applicable, ISO/IEC 27701:2019 was designed to support compliance with privacy law but is not a substitute for it. A revised edition was published in 2025 with an expanded and re-numbered Annex A, including controls on privacy by design, data subject rights and awareness; confirm the current edition and its control numbering before citing the 2019 control set, and expect existing certificates to migrate over time.

items.title: ISO 22301:2019 - Security and resilience - Business continuity management systems - Requirements
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO)
items.applicability: Organisations that need to plan for, respond to and recover from disruptive incidents - cyber attack, data loss, supplier failure, site loss or regional outage. It specifies requirements for a business continuity management system, including business impact analysis, continuity strategies, recovery objectives, exercising and auditing of the continuity arrangements, and is the most widely recognised certifiable continuity standard. It aligns with ISO/IEC 27001 Annex SL, ISO 31000 and the contingency planning guidance in NIST SP 800-34.
items.notes: Superseded ISO 22301:2012. Certification is granted for a three-year cycle with surveillance audits; the standard explicitly supports joint ISO 22301 and ISO/IEC 27001 certification, where the business impact analysis and continuity plans serve both schemes. Whether the standard covers physical safety as well as information security is a common point of confusion with ISO 22320 (security and resilience - emergency management) and ISO 22313.

items.title: ISO 31000:2018 - Risk management - Guidelines
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO)
items.applicability: Generic guidance for organisations of any size and sector on establishing, operating and improving a risk management framework, built on a 10-principle model and a six-step process (context, risk assessment, risk treatment, monitoring, communication and consultation, and recording/reporting). It is the risk backbone used by ISO/IEC 27001 clause 4.5, ISO 22301 and ISO 37301, and by auditors of enterprise risk programmes. It is explicitly a guidance document: ISO does not offer certification against ISO 31000.
items.notes: Superseded ISO 31000:2009. The 2018 edition replaced the 2009 process model with ten principles and three dimensions (principles, framework and process), and its definitions of risk, risk appetite and risk treatment differ subtly from ISO/IEC 27005 and from COSO. The standard carries an explicit disclaimer that it is not suitable for certification purposes and for regulated sectors requiring specific regulatory compliance.

items.title: ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 and ITIL 4 - IT service management requirements and practice guidance
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO); AXELOS (now PeopleCert) for ITIL 4
items.applicability: ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 is the certifiable requirements standard for an IT service management system, covering service management system requirements, service management practices, new and changed services and service transition. ITIL 4 is the accompanying non-certifiable practice guidance with a value-chain based approach to service design, transition, operation and continual improvement. Together they give IT and service desk functions a common operating model that GRC teams usually connect to incident, change, problem and continuity data.
items.notes: ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 superseded ISO/IEC 20000-1:2011 and the service management system guidance in ISO/IEC 20000-2, which was withdrawn in 2018 and whose content now sits mainly in ITIL 4. ITIL 4 replaced ITIL v3 (2011) and is a licensed publication; PeopleCert and Axelos materials remain copyrighted and should not be reproduced in internal training material.

items.title: ISO 9001:2015 and ISO 37301:2020 - Quality management and compliance management system requirements
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO)
items.applicability: ISO 9001:2015 is the quality management system standard used where customer, product or service quality is managed through documented processes, audits and corrective action - often the operating system that a compliance or security function plugs into. ISO 37301:2020 is the compliance management system standard, covering an organisation's obligations, compliance risk assessment, compliance controls, monitoring, reporting and improvement. Both are certifiable and are frequently used together in regulated organisations.
items.notes: ISO 37301:2020 superseded and withdrew ISO 19600:2015 (compliance management systems), so any reference to an 'ISO 19600 compliance management system' today refers to a withdrawn edition. ISO 9001:2015 is under revision with a new edition expected in 2026, so confirm the current edition and clause numbering before citing it in an audit programme. Companion page for ISO 37301:2020 is https://www.iso.org/standard/75057.html.

items.title: ISO 37001:2018 - Anti-bribery management systems - Requirements
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO)
items.applicability: Organisations in any sector that need to prevent, detect and respond to bribery and corruption risk, including third-party bribery. It requires an anti-bribery management system with leadership accountability, risk assessment, controls, due diligence on third parties, training, monitoring, reporting and investigation, and it is certifiable. It is regularly paired with ISO 37001-adjacent due diligence regimes such as the UK Bribery Act and the FCPA.
items.notes: First edition, published in 2018 and aligned to ISO 19011:2018 for audit and certification. ISO published ISO 37002:2025 as guidance on anti-bribery management systems, which supplements rather than replaces the requirements standard. Certification requires a two-stage audit and is available through accredited bodies.

items.title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 - Information technology - Artificial intelligence - Management system
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC)
items.applicability: Organisations that develop, deploy, use or supply artificial intelligence systems and want a certifiable management system covering AI governance, AI impact assessment, data quality and provenance, transparency, human oversight, and monitoring of AI system behaviour. It was published in December 2023 in response to demand from both regulators and procurement teams, and is positioned as complementary to, not a substitute for, the EU AI Act's legal obligations. Certification is available through accredited bodies.
items.notes: First edition, the first ISO/IEC standard dedicated to AI management systems, structured on Annex SL so it can be integrated with ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO 9001. Its management system requirements are broadly compatible with the EU AI Act's obligations but do not implement them; the Act's own phased application dates and any implementing acts take precedence. Adoption and accredited certification capacity are still growing, so expect schedules to vary by country.

items.title: ISO 19600:2021 - Sustainability reporting - Guidance on the assurance of sustainability-related information
items.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO)
items.applicability: Guidance for organisations and their assurance providers on the assurance of sustainability-related information, covering the principles and criteria used in an assurance engagement (principles of assurance, an assurance process, the sufficiency of evidence and a clear assurance conclusion) together with sustainability reporting and management system guidance. It is relevant to GRC practitioners because it defines assurance concepts in the same vocabulary as financial and IT assurance, and it informs assurance readiness for CSRD and related reporting.
items.notes: Important numbering trap: the standard number ISO 19600 was previously used for 'Compliance management systems - Guidelines' (ISO 19600:2015), which was withdrawn and superseded by ISO 37301:2020. ISO 19600:2021 is the sustainability assurance standard. Any internal document that cites 'ISO 19600 compliance management' is referencing the withdrawn 2015 edition and should be corrected to ISO 37301:2020.

items.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
items.applicability: A voluntary, outcome-based framework for any organisation that wants to understand and manage its cybersecurity risk, structured as six Functions - Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover - with 23 categories and more than 100 subcategories written as desired outcomes rather than requirements. CSF 2.0 added the Govern function, which is what makes it usable as a governance and reporting instrument alongside risk and compliance work, and it explicitly covers organisational risk management and supply chain risk. It is not a control catalogue and cannot be certified.
items.notes: Supersedes NIST CSF 1.1. Published alongside CSF 2.0 were the Quick Start Guide for CSF 2.0 (for small and medium organisations) and a Community Profile for Cyber AI. NIST has continued work on CSF 2.0 profiles and revisions, so confirm the current revision, the available profiles and whether a specific subcategory has been reworded before quoting text in an audit or contractual annex.

items.title: NIST SP 800-37 Revision 2 - Risk Management Framework (RMF) for Information Systems and Organizations
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
items.applicability: The Risk Management Framework organises the full lifecycle of managing federal information system risk through seven tasks - Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize and Monitor - with each task supported by the SP 800-53 control baselines and SP 800-30 assessment procedures. It was written for federal agencies, but it is the most widely adopted risk lifecycle model in commercial practice, where it is usually paired with an authorisation decision recorded as an Authority to Operate.
items.notes: Revision 2 (December 2018) followed the 2017 update that removed the security control overlay approach and introduced the Prepare task, the new authorisation step and the seven-task structure. A further revision has been in draft and public comment for some time, so confirm the current revision and task numbering with NIST before citing a specific task as authoritative; existing programmes commonly reference the Revision 2 task numbers as the de facto standard.

items.title: NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5 - Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
items.applicability: The control catalogue from which nearly all US federal information systems are built, and the most reused control baseline in private-sector GRC programmes. Revision 5 introduced the 'well-understood' tailoring overlay, control enhancements written as testable enhancements, and the low/moderate/high impact baselines published separately in SP 800-53B. It is the source for OSCAL machine-readable control definitions used in automation and assessment evidence pipelines.
items.notes: Supersedes Revision 4. Revision 5 was published in September 2020, updated in December 2020 (update 1) and again with the 5.2.0 control catalog in December 2023. A further revision went to public comment during 2025, so confirm the current revision and the exact enhancement numbers before citing a control in an audit or contract; control text and numbering have also shifted between the 5.1.0 and 5.2.0 releases.

items.title: NIST SP 800-30 Revision 1 - Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
items.applicability: The methodological guide for conducting information security risk assessments, covering the preparation, conduct and maintenance phases, threat source and vulnerability identification, likelihood and impact determination, risk estimation and the resulting risk response. It supports both the RMF assessment step and the organisation-level risk management process in SP 800-39. It is guidance rather than a control baseline, and it is the reference most auditors expect to see behind a documented risk assessment.
items.notes: Revision 1 aligned the assessment method with SP 800-39 and the RMF, adding the organisation-level and system-level risk assessment distinction and an approach to assessment tiers. Errata have been issued against the publication. Revisions to SP 800-30 have been discussed as part of the wider RMF update, so confirm the current revision before treating it as the only sanctioned assessment methodology.

items.title: NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 - Incident Handling Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management: A CSF 2.0 Community Profile
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
items.applicability: The reference for building and running an incident response capability, now restructured around the CSF 2.0 functions so that incident handling is expressed as Detect, Respond and Recover outcomes that link back to governance and organisational context. It applies to any organisation operating a security operations function, a managed detection and response service or a documented incident response process, and it is the natural counterpart to ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A clauses A.5.24 to A.5.28.
items.notes: Revision 3 (April 2025) supersedes Revision 2 (August 2012 plus 2017 errata) and replaces the incident response lifecycle with a CSF 2.0-aligned structure; practitioners who trained on the Revision 2 lifecycle should check the new document rather than assume continuity of section numbers.

items.title: NIST SP 800-34 Revision 1 - Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Processing Systems
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
items.applicability: The contingency planning guidance behind FIPS 199 (federal information processing standards) and FIPS 200 (minimum security requirements for federal information systems), covering the four-step contingency planning process (contingency planning strategy, contingency plan development, testing and training, and plan maintenance) and the seven elements of a contingency plan. It remains the most widely referenced technical methodology for information system continuity planning and is the natural counterpart to ISO 22301.
items.notes: Revision 1 (May 2010) remains the published revision of this document and is still routinely cited, although it predates the CSF 2.0 and the RMF updates and its language (for example information system contingency planning) is dated by comparison. NIST has signalled continued work in the contingency and continuity guidance area, so confirm the current revision before citing it as the only authoritative methodology.

items.title: NIST SP 800-39 and NIST SP 800-137 - Managing Information Security Risk and Information Security Continuous Monitoring
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
items.edition: SP 800-39 (2011) and SP 800-137 (2011), both initial final releases
items.applicability: SP 800-39 establishes the organisation-level and system-level risk management processes that the RMF operationalises, covering framing, assessment, response and monitoring of information security risk. SP 800-137 defines an information security continuous monitoring (ISCM) strategy with three organisational tiers (governance, operational, measurement and analysis) and an ongoing metrics programme. Together they are the standard reference for how an enterprise risk function monitors control effectiveness on an ongoing basis.
items.notes: SP 800-39 was published in March 2011 and SP 800-137 in September 2011; a revision of SP 800-39 has been in progress for some years, so confirm the current revision on the NIST CSRC publications page. Companion page for SP 800-137 is https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/137/final. Both documents predate CSF 2.0 and the RMF Revision 2 task structure and are usually read alongside them.
